claim: Planarians are capable of whole-body regeneration.
source: Planarians are capable of whole-body regeneration and mount distinct molecular responses to wounds that result in tissue absence and those that do not.
evidence: This is a well-established fact stated in the abstract and supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Planarians mount distinct molecular responses to wounds that result in tissue absence versus those that do not.
source: Planarians are capable of whole-body regeneration and mount distinct molecular responses to wounds that result in tissue absence and those that do not.
evidence: This claim is supported by prior work cited in the manuscript (Wenemoser and Reddien, 2010; Wenemoser et al., 2012).

claim: Smed-follistatin is required for planarian regeneration.
source: We describe a follistatin homolog (Smed-follistatin) required for planarian regeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that fst(RNAi) animals fail to regenerate.

claim: Smed-follistatin inhibition blocks responses to tissue absence but does not prevent normal tissue turnover.
source: Smed-follistatin inhibition blocks responses to tissue absence but does not prevent normal tissue turnover.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing fst(RNAi) animals fail to regenerate but maintain normal tissue homeostasis.

claim: Two activin homologs (Smed-activin-1 and Smed-activin-2) are required for the Smed-follistatin phenotype.
source: Two activin homologs (Smed-activin-1 and Smed-activin-2) are required for the Smed-follistatin phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by RNAi suppression experiments showing that act-1 or act-2 RNAi suppresses the fst(RNAi) phenotype.

claim: Smed-follistatin is wound-induced.
source: Finally, Smed-follistatin is wound-induced and expressed at higher levels following injuries that cause tissue absence.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data showing fst expression increases at wounds.

claim: Smed-follistatin is expressed at higher levels following injuries that cause tissue absence.
source: Finally, Smed-follistatin is wound-induced and expressed at higher levels following injuries that cause tissue absence.
evidence: This is supported by comparing fst expression after incision versus wedge excision.

claim: Smed-follistatin inhibits Smed-Activin proteins to trigger regeneration specifically following injuries involving tissue absence.
source: These data suggest that Smed-follistatin inhibits Smed-Activin proteins to trigger regeneration specifically following injuries involving tissue absence and identify a mechanism critical for regeneration initiation, a process important across the animal kingdom.
evidence: This is a model inferred from the genetic interaction data and expression patterns.

claim: Hydra are capable of whole-animal regeneration from tissue fragments.
source: Invertebrates such as Hydra are capable of whole-animal regeneration from tissue fragments, and many vertebrates can regenerate appendages or repair damaged organs (Sánchez Alvarado, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sánchez Alvarado, 2000.

claim: Many vertebrates can regenerate appendages or repair damaged organs.
source: Invertebrates such as Hydra are capable of whole-animal regeneration from tissue fragments, and many vertebrates can regenerate appendages or repair damaged organs (Sánchez Alvarado, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sánchez Alvarado, 2000.

claim: The central mechanisms that drive regeneration are poorly understood.
source: Despite this widespread relevance, the central mechanisms that drive regeneration are poorly understood.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of the field.

claim: Planarians are flatworms capable of regeneration following an almost limitless variety of injuries.
source: Planarians are flatworms capable of regeneration following an almost limitless variety of injuries and have emerged as a powerful model for exploring the molecular underpinnings of regeneration (Newmark and Sánchez Alvarado, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Newmark and Sánchez Alvarado, 2002.

claim: Planarians have emerged as a powerful model for exploring the molecular underpinnings of regeneration.
source: Planarians are flatworms capable of regeneration following an almost limitless variety of injuries and have emerged as a powerful model for exploring the molecular underpinnings of regeneration (Newmark and Sánchez Alvarado, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Newmark and Sánchez Alvarado, 2002.

claim: New tissues are formed at planarian wound sites in a process called blastema formation.
source: New tissues are formed at planarian wound sites in a process called blastema formation, and pre-existing tissues are reorganized after amputation to accommodate reduced animal size and further generate missing tissues (Morgan, 1901; Reddien and Sánchez Alvarado, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Morgan, 1901 and Reddien and Sánchez Alvarado, 2004.

claim: Pre-existing tissues are reorganized after amputation to accommodate reduced animal size and further generate missing tissues.
source: New tissues are formed at planarian wound sites in a process called blastema formation, and pre-existing tissues are reorganized after amputation to accommodate reduced animal size and further generate missing tissues (Morgan, 1901; Reddien and Sánchez Alvarado, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Morgan, 1901 and Reddien and Sánchez Alvarado, 2004.

claim: The source of regenerated tissue in planarians is a population of adult dividing cells called neoblasts.
source: The source of regenerated tissue in planarians is a population of adult dividing cells called neoblasts (Reddien and Sánchez Alvarado, 2004), which include pluripotent stem cells called clonogenic neoblasts (cNeoblasts) (Wagner et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Reddien and Sánchez Alvarado, 2004 and Wagner et al., 2011.

claim: Neoblasts include pluripotent stem cells called clonogenic neoblasts (cNeoblasts).
source: The source of regenerated tissue in planarians is a population of adult dividing cells called neoblasts (Reddien and Sánchez Alvarado, 2004), which include pluripotent stem cells called clonogenic neoblasts (cNeoblasts) (Wagner et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wagner et al., 2011.

claim: Neoblasts are the only somatic cycling cells in adult animals.
source: Neoblasts are the only somatic cycling cells in adult animals and can be specifically ablated by gamma irradiation, allowing for dissection of the requirements for neoblasts in regenerative processes (Reddien and Sánchez Alvarado, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Reddien and Sánchez Alvarado, 2004.

claim: Neoblasts can be specifically ablated by gamma irradiation.
source: Neoblasts are the only somatic cycling cells in adult animals and can be specifically ablated by gamma irradiation, allowing for dissection of the requirements for neoblasts in regenerative processes (Reddien and Sánchez Alvarado, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Reddien and Sánchez Alvarado, 2004.

claim: Animals initiate distinct cellular and molecular responses to 'major injuries' that remove significant amounts of tissue and to 'simple injuries' that require only minimal healing for repair.
source: One finding to emerge from this work is that animals initiate distinct cellular and molecular responses to 'major injuries' that remove significant amounts of tissue (e.g., head amputation) and to 'simple injuries' that require only minimal healing for repair (wounds that do not elicit blastema formation, such as punctures or incisions).
evidence: This is supported by prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: Following simple injury, animals display an increase in mitotic numbers 6 hr after injury before returning to baseline levels.
source: Following simple injury, for example, animals display an increase in mitotic numbers 6 hr after injury before returning to baseline levels (Wenemoser and Reddien, 2010), and expression of numerous wound-induced genes becomes undetectable by 24 hr after injury (Wenemoser et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wenemoser and Reddien, 2010.

claim: Expression of numerous wound-induced genes becomes undetectable by 24 hr after simple injury.
source: Following simple injury, for example, animals display an increase in mitotic numbers 6 hr after injury before returning to baseline levels (Wenemoser and Reddien, 2010), and expression of numerous wound-induced genes becomes undetectable by 24 hr after injury (Wenemoser et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wenemoser et al., 2012.

claim: Following a major injury, the 6 hr increase in mitotic numbers is followed by a second increase 48 hr after amputation.
source: Following a major injury, these same initial responses are observed, but subsequent responses are also activated: the 6 hr increase in mitotic numbers is followed by a second increase 48 hr after amputation (Wenemoser and Reddien, 2010), and wound-induced gene expression persists beyond 24 hr and is refined over several days (Wenemoser et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wenemoser and Reddien, 2010.

claim: Following a major injury, wound-induced gene expression persists beyond 24 hr and is refined over several days.
source: Following a major injury, these same initial responses are observed, but subsequent responses are also activated: the 6 hr increase in mitotic numbers is followed by a second increase 48 hr after amputation (Wenemoser and Reddien, 2010), and wound-induced gene expression persists beyond 24 hr and is refined over several days (Wenemoser et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wenemoser et al., 2012.

claim: Inhibition of Smed-follistatin with RNA interference completely blocked regeneration.
source: Inhibition of Smed-follistatin (follistatin or fst), a gene encoding a Follistatin-like TGF-β-superfamily inhibitor, completely blocked regeneration (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: No brain regeneration or anterior pole regeneration was observed in fst(RNAi) animals.
source: No brain regeneration or anterior pole regeneration was observed in fst(RNAi) animals (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: fst(RNAi) animals failed to produce a blastema following tail amputation.
source: fst(RNAi) animals, however, also failed to produce a blastema following either tail amputation or the excision of lateral tissue wedges that left anterior and posterior poles intact (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: fst(RNAi) animals failed to produce a blastema following the excision of lateral tissue wedges that left anterior and posterior poles intact.
source: fst(RNAi) animals, however, also failed to produce a blastema following either tail amputation or the excision of lateral tissue wedges that left anterior and posterior poles intact (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: fst is required broadly for regeneration.
source: These data demonstrate that fst is required broadly for regeneration.
evidence: This is inferred from the multiple regeneration defects observed in fst(RNAi) animals.

claim: Unamputated fst(RNAi) animals did not shrink or lose structures, even after several months of significant expression reduction with RNAi.
source: Strikingly, unamputated fst(RNAi) animals did not shrink or lose structures, as is typically seen in animals with neoblast dysfunction, even after several months of significant expression reduction with RNAi (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Amputated fst(RNAi) animals displayed ongoing long-term neoblast-based tissue turnover of remaining tissue despite failing to regenerate.
source: Furthermore, amputated animals—despite failing to regenerate—displayed ongoing long-term neoblast-based tissue turnover of remaining tissue (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The requirement for fst in tissue replacement is specific to regeneration, as it is not detectably required for neoblast-mediated tissue turnover.
source: Together, these data suggest that the requirement for fst in tissue replacement is specific to regeneration, as it is not detectably required for neoblast-mediated tissue turnover.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that fst(RNAi) animals maintain tissue turnover but fail to regenerate.

claim: fst expression was induced at wounds by 6 hr following amputation.
source: fst expression was induced at wounds by 6 hr following amputation (Wenemoser et al., 2012; Roberts-Galbraith and Newmark, 2013) and persisted for several days, with maximal expression around 12 hr post-amputation (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by citations and experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: fst expression persisted for several days after amputation, with maximal expression around 12 hr post-amputation.
source: fst expression was induced at wounds by 6 hr following amputation (Wenemoser et al., 2012; Roberts-Galbraith and Newmark, 2013) and persisted for several days, with maximal expression around 12 hr post-amputation (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: In unamputated animals, fst was expressed sparsely throughout the animal, including ventrally, in a thin peripheral domain, and at the anterior pole.
source: In unamputated animals, fst was expressed sparsely throughout the animal, including ventrally, in a thin peripheral domain, and at the anterior pole (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 4; Roberts-Galbraith and Newmark, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 4, and a citation.

claim: Injection of fst dsRNA only after amputation caused poor blastema formation and regeneration defects.
source: Injection of fst dsRNA only after amputation caused poor blastema formation and regeneration defects (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), consistent with a requirement for wound-induced fst expression in regeneration.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: fst is a wound-induced factor required for regeneration.
source: We conclude that fst is a wound-induced factor required for regeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: fst(RNAi) animals displayed normal neoblast numbers prior to amputation.
source: fst(RNAi) animals displayed normal neoblast numbers prior to amputation, indicating that the observed regeneration failure is not caused by neoblast loss (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The neoblast response to injury involves two peaks (6 hr and 48 hr post-amputation) in mitotic cell numbers.
source: The neoblast response to injury involves two peaks (6 hr and 48 hr post-amputation) in mitotic cell numbers, in between which neoblasts migrate to wounds (Wenemoser and Reddien, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wenemoser and Reddien, 2010.

claim: The first mitotic peak is generically induced by all injury types and is spatially widespread.
source: The first peak is generically induced by all injury types and is spatially widespread (Wenemoser and Reddien, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wenemoser and Reddien, 2010.

claim: The second mitotic peak occurs specifically following major injuries (removing tissues) and is biased toward wound sites.
source: The second peak occurs specifically following major injuries (removing tissues) and is biased toward wound sites (Wenemoser and Reddien, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wenemoser and Reddien, 2010.

claim: Amputated fst(RNAi) animals displayed a normal 6 hr mitotic peak.
source: Amputated fst(RNAi) animals displayed a normal 6 hr mitotic peak, indicating that a normal generic injury response was present (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Amputated fst(RNAi) animals failed to display a 48 hr mitotic peak.
source: By contrast, these animals failed to display a 48 hr mitotic peak (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: fst(RNAi) animals displayed localization of mitoses toward wound sites 48 hr after amputation.
source: fst(RNAi) animals did however display localization of mitoses toward wound sites 48 hr after amputation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and neoblast enrichment at wound sites 18 hr after injury (Figure 2C), indicating that neoblast migration occurred normally.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: fst(RNAi) animals displayed neoblast enrichment at wound sites 18 hr after injury.
source: fst(RNAi) animals did however display localization of mitoses toward wound sites 48 hr after amputation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and neoblast enrichment at wound sites 18 hr after injury (Figure 2C), indicating that neoblast migration occurred normally.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Neoblast migration occurred normally in fst(RNAi) animals.
source: fst(RNAi) animals did however display localization of mitoses toward wound sites 48 hr after amputation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and neoblast enrichment at wound sites 18 hr after injury (Figure 2C), indicating that neoblast migration occurred normally.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of neoblast enrichment at wounds.

claim: Head amputation normally induces neoblasts to produce ovo+ eye progenitors.
source: Head amputation normally induces neoblasts to produce ovo+ eye progenitors (Lapan and Reddien, 2012), but this process failed in fst(RNAi) animals (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lapan and Reddien, 2012.

claim: Production of ovo+ eye progenitors failed in fst(RNAi) animals.
source: Head amputation normally induces neoblasts to produce ovo+ eye progenitors (Lapan and Reddien, 2012), but this process failed in fst(RNAi) animals (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: fst is required for several aspects of the regeneration-specific neoblast response to injury.
source: From these data taken together, we conclude that fst is required for several aspects of the regeneration-specific neoblast response to injury.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: Apoptosis increases following injury in planarians.
source: Apoptosis increases following injury in planarians (Pellettieri et al., 2010), and, like the mitotic response, this increase involves a generic injury phase and a missing-tissue-specific phase.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pellettieri et al., 2010.

claim: A local apoptosis burst occurs at wound sites 4 hr following any injury.
source: First, a local apoptosis burst occurs at wound sites 4 hr following any injury; second, a body-wide apoptosis burst occurs 72 hr after injury, but only in cases involving missing tissue (Pellettieri et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pellettieri et al., 2010.

claim: A body-wide apoptosis burst occurs 72 hr after injury, but only in cases involving missing tissue.
source: First, a local apoptosis burst occurs at wound sites 4 hr following any injury; second, a body-wide apoptosis burst occurs 72 hr after injury, but only in cases involving missing tissue (Pellettieri et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pellettieri et al., 2010.

claim: The apoptosis level in the 72 hr phase scales with the amount of missing tissue.
source: The apoptosis level in this latter phase scales with the amount of missing tissue (Pellettieri et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pellettieri et al., 2010.

claim: fst(RNAi) pharynges displayed little increase in apoptotic cell numbers 72 hr post amputation.
source: Strikingly, fst(RNAi) pharynges displayed little increase in apoptotic cell numbers 72 hr post amputation, whereas a roughly 20-fold increase from pre-amputation levels occurred in control pharynges (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Control pharynges displayed a roughly 20-fold increase in apoptotic cell numbers 72 hr post amputation from pre-amputation levels.
source: Strikingly, fst(RNAi) pharynges displayed little increase in apoptotic cell numbers 72 hr post amputation, whereas a roughly 20-fold increase from pre-amputation levels occurred in control pharynges (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: fst(RNAi) animals had a normal 4 hr apoptosis burst.
source: fst(RNAi) animals had a normal 4 hr apoptosis burst, indicating that fst is not generally required for apoptosis (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The 72 hr apoptotic response occurs in animals that have had their neoblasts ablated and cannot regenerate.
source: The 72 hr apoptotic response occurs in animals that have had their neoblasts ablated and cannot regenerate (Pellettieri et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pellettieri et al., 2010.

claim: The failure of fst(RNAi) animals to produce the 72 hr apoptotic response cannot be explained as a non-specific result of regeneration failure.
source: Therefore, the failure of fst(RNAi) animals to produce this response cannot be explained as a non-specific result of regeneration failure.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that irradiated animals display the 72 hr apoptotic response despite being unable to regenerate.

claim: fst(RNAi) animals displayed normal wound-induced gene expression 3 hr and 6 hr after amputation.
source: fst(RNAi) animals displayed normal wound-induced gene expression 3 hr and 6 hr after amputation (jun-1: n = 20/20, nlg1: n = 5/5) but reduced expression compared to controls 24–48 hr after amputation (arrows; jun-1: 17/19 correctly scored blindly, p<0.01 Fisher's exact test, nlg1: 22/27 correctly scored blindly, p<0.01, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: fst(RNAi) animals displayed reduced wound-induced gene expression compared to controls 24–48 hr after amputation.
source: fst(RNAi) animals displayed normal wound-induced gene expression 3 hr and 6 hr after amputation (jun-1: n = 20/20, nlg1: n = 5/5) but reduced expression compared to controls 24–48 hr after amputation (arrows; jun-1: 17/19 correctly scored blindly, p<0.01 Fisher's exact test, nlg1: 22/27 correctly scored blindly, p<0.01, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Some wound-induced genes display expression that inversely scales with missing tissue amount.
source: Notably, some wound-induced genes display expression that inversely scales with missing tissue amount; for example, Smed-delta-1 displays higher expression after an incision or puncture (simple injuries) than after amputation (a major injury) (Wenemoser et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wenemoser et al., 2012.

claim: Smed-delta-1 displays higher expression after an incision or puncture (simple injuries) than after amputation (a major injury).
source: Notably, some wound-induced genes display expression that inversely scales with missing tissue amount; for example, Smed-delta-1 displays higher expression after an incision or puncture (simple injuries) than after amputation (a major injury) (Wenemoser et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wenemoser et al., 2012.

claim: Amputated fst(RNAi) animals displayed a higher level of Smed-delta-1 expression than did controls 24 hr after amputation.
source: Amputated fst(RNAi) animals displayed a higher, rather than lower, level of Smed-delta-1 expression than did controls 24 hr after amputation (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The lower expression levels observed for other wound-induced genes in fst(RNAi) animals do not reflect generically lower gene expression at wounds, but instead a specific requirement for fst for missing-tissue-specific gene expression.
source: Therefore, the lower expression levels observed for other wound-induced genes in fst(RNAi) animals do not reflect generically lower gene expression at wounds, but instead a specific requirement for fst for missing-tissue-specific gene expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that delta-1 expression is higher in fst(RNAi) animals.

claim: wntP-2 is normally expressed in planarian tails.
source: For example, wntP-2 (also known as wnt11-5 [Gurley et al., 2010]) is normally expressed in planarian tails (Petersen and Reddien, 2009; Gurley et al., 2010) and its expression domain restricts posteriorly within 48 hr of amputation whether regeneration proceeds or not (Gurley et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Petersen and Reddien, 2009 and Gurley et al., 2010.

claim: The wntP-2 expression domain restricts posteriorly within 48 hr of amputation whether regeneration proceeds or not.
source: For example, wntP-2 (also known as wnt11-5 [Gurley et al., 2010]) is normally expressed in planarian tails (Petersen and Reddien, 2009; Gurley et al., 2010) and its expression domain restricts posteriorly within 48 hr of amputation whether regeneration proceeds or not (Gurley et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gurley et al., 2010.

claim: fst(RNAi) animals did not rescale the wntP-2 expression domain 48 hr following amputation.
source: fst(RNAi) animals did not rescale the wntP-2 expression domain 48 hr following amputation, further supporting a model in which fst is required for responding to missing tissue (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Following head amputation, head fragments reduce numbers of anterior-specific cell types.
source: Following head amputation, head fragments not only produce posterior-specific cell types but also reduce numbers of anterior-specific cell types (which are overabundant for the new fragment dimensions). This process failed in fst(RNAi) head fragments (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The process of reducing numbers of anterior-specific cell types failed in fst(RNAi) head fragments.
source: Following head amputation, head fragments not only produce posterior-specific cell types but also reduce numbers of anterior-specific cell types (which are overabundant for the new fragment dimensions). This process failed in fst(RNAi) head fragments (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: fst(RNAi) fragments did not produce pharynges de novo.
source: Finally, fst(RNAi) fragments did not produce pharynges de novo (which normally occurs in pre-existing head and tail fragment tissue) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: RNAi of smad1 blocked blastema formation but did not block pharynx formation.
source: By contrast, RNAi of a different gene that blocked blastema formation (smad1) did not block pharynx formation, indicating this defect is not a simple consequence of blastema formation failure (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: fst is required broadly for missing-tissue-specific wound responses.
source: We conclude that fst is required broadly for missing-tissue-specific wound responses, and that these defects likely underlie the inability of fst(RNAi) animals to regenerate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: Follistatin proteins are well-characterized extracellular inhibitors of TGF-β ligands.
source: Because Follistatin proteins are well-characterized extracellular inhibitors of TGF-β ligands (Nakamura et al., 1990; Hemmati-Brivanlou et al., 1994), we sought to identify putative TGF-β ligands that Smed-Follistatin might regulate to promote regeneration.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nakamura et al., 1990 and Hemmati-Brivanlou et al., 1994.

claim: Seven putative TGF-β superfamily members exist in the Schmidtea mediterranea genome.
source: Seven putative TGF-β superfamily members exist in the Schmidtea mediterranea genome (Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Molina et al., 2007; Orii and Watanabe, 2007; Reddien et al., 2007; Gaviño and Reddien, 2011; Molina et al., 2011; Wenemoser et al., 2012; Roberts-Galbraith and Newmark, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations and phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: RNAi of Smed-activin-1 strongly suppressed the blastema formation defect of fst(RNAi) animals.
source: We tested this possibility (see Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and 'Materials and methods' for details) and found that RNAi of either of two genes, Smed-activin-1 (act-1 in short) or Smed-activin-2 (act-2), strongly suppressed the blastema formation defect (Figure 4A), the failure to regenerate a brain (Figure 4A), and the failed missing-tissue apoptotic response of fst(RNAi) animals (Figure 4B); RNAi of act-2 can also restore anterior pole regeneration in fst(RNAi) animals (Roberts-Galbraith and Newmark, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: RNAi of Smed-activin-2 strongly suppressed the blastema formation defect of fst(RNAi) animals.
source: We tested this possibility (see Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and 'Materials and methods' for details) and found that RNAi of either of two genes, Smed-activin-1 (act-1 in short) or Smed-activin-2 (act-2), strongly suppressed the blastema formation defect (Figure 4A), the failure to regenerate a brain (Figure 4A), and the failed missing-tissue apoptotic response of fst(RNAi) animals (Figure 4B); RNAi of act-2 can also restore anterior pole regeneration in fst(RNAi) animals (Roberts-Galbraith and Newmark, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: RNAi of act-1 or act-2 strongly suppressed the failure to regenerate a brain in fst(RNAi) animals.
source: We tested this possibility (see Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and 'Materials and methods' for details) and found that RNAi of either of two genes, Smed-activin-1 (act-1 in short) or Smed-activin-2 (act-2), strongly suppressed the blastema formation defect (Figure 4A), the failure to regenerate a brain (Figure 4A), and the failed missing-tissue apoptotic response of fst(RNAi) animals (Figure 4B); RNAi of act-2 can also restore anterior pole regeneration in fst(RNAi) animals (Roberts-Galbraith and Newmark, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: RNAi of act-1 or act-2 strongly suppressed the failed missing-tissue apoptotic response of fst(RNAi) animals.
source: We tested this possibility (see Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and 'Materials and methods' for details) and found that RNAi of either of two genes, Smed-activin-1 (act-1 in short) or Smed-activin-2 (act-2), strongly suppressed the blastema formation defect (Figure 4A), the failure to regenerate a brain (Figure 4A), and the failed missing-tissue apoptotic response of fst(RNAi) animals (Figure 4B); RNAi of act-2 can also restore anterior pole regeneration in fst(RNAi) animals (Roberts-Galbraith and Newmark, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: RNAi of act-2 can restore anterior pole regeneration in fst(RNAi) animals.
source: We tested this possibility (see Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and 'Materials and methods' for details) and found that RNAi of either of two genes, Smed-activin-1 (act-1 in short) or Smed-activin-2 (act-2), strongly suppressed the blastema formation defect (Figure 4A), the failure to regenerate a brain (Figure 4A), and the failed missing-tissue apoptotic response of fst(RNAi) animals (Figure 4B); RNAi of act-2 can also restore anterior pole regeneration in fst(RNAi) animals (Roberts-Galbraith and Newmark, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Roberts-Galbraith and Newmark, 2013.

claim: Follistatin proteins can directly regulate Activin proteins in other organisms.
source: Given that Follistatin proteins can directly regulate Activin proteins in other organisms (Nakamura et al., 1990; Hemmati-Brivanlou et al., 1994), these data suggest that Follistatin promotes missing tissue responses by inhibiting the function of Activin proteins.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nakamura et al., 1990 and Hemmati-Brivanlou et al., 1994.

claim: Follistatin promotes missing tissue responses by inhibiting the function of Activin proteins.
source: Given that Follistatin proteins can directly regulate Activin proteins in other organisms (Nakamura et al., 1990; Hemmati-Brivanlou et al., 1994), these data suggest that Follistatin promotes missing tissue responses by inhibiting the function of Activin proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic interaction data and known biochemical interactions.

claim: act-1(RNAi) animals were capable of regenerating.

claim: Increased act-1 expression was not detected following either incision or tissue wedge excision.

claim: act-1 expression was detected throughout the intestine of uninjured animals, suggesting an intestinal source of Activin-1 protein.

claim: TGF-β signaling is involved in axolotl limb regeneration.
source: Interestingly, a number of systems use TGF-β signaling to promote rather than suppress regeneration: TGF-β signaling is involved in axolotl limb and Xenopus tail regeneration (Lévesque et al., 2007; Ho and Whitman, 2008), activin expression can be induced by wounding and exogenous TGF-β can speed healing in mammals (Mustoe et al., 1987; Hübner et al., 1996; Sulyok et al., 2004), TGF-β signaling can promote regeneration following mouse ear hole-punching (Liu et al., 2011), and wound-induced activin promotes cell proliferation and migration following zebrafish fin amputation (Jaźwińska et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lévesque et al., 2007.
